info.title: OpenType API
info.description: HTTP edge for the OpenType service. Routes are added as their readiness checks land; a documented route is not a claim that a provider, database, or accelerator is live.

get.summary:
Liveness. Public and unauthenticated: it reports that the process is up, not
that any dependency is ready.

Readiness. Every dependency that is required to serve traffic must pass here
before this returns `200`; an absent dependency keeps the instance out of
rotation rather than letting a request fail downstream.

Refuses: a scope the calling account does not itself hold (`403`), an empty
scope list (`400`), and a service-account principal when the caller cannot
write members (`403`) — minting an organization-owned credential is an
administrative act, not a personal one.

post.summary: Issues a new secret for an existing key and returns it once.
post.description:
The old secret stops working immediately. There is no overlap window, which
means a rotation is a brief outage for anything still presenting the old
value.

ponytail: no grace period. Two live secrets per key would let a deployment
roll without downtime, and it needs a second `(hash, prefix, expires_at)`
triple on the row plus verification against both. Add it when a customer
rotates a key that more than one process holds; until then, the simple
version is the one that cannot leave a forgotten second credential valid.

Refuses to rotate a revoked key (`409`): revocation is a security decision
and rotating past it would quietly undo it.

delete.summary:
Removes a member and revokes every key that acted as them, in one
transaction.
delete.description:
Those two must commit together. A removal that commits without the
revocations leaves a departed person holding live credentials, which is the
exact failure offboarding exists to prevent; a revocation that commits
without the removal leaves a member who cannot work and looks like a bug.

Refuses three things: a target role above the caller's own, acting on a
member who already outranks the caller, and demoting the last owner. The
last one is not a permission check — it is the check that stops an
organization from locking itself out with a single `PATCH`.

post.summary: Submits a run and returns its verdict or its decision.
post.description:
Refuses: a body over [`MAX_BODY_BYTES`] (`413`), a missing or malformed
`Idempotency-Key` (`400`), a verdict schema outside the bounds (`400`,
`invalid_verdict_schema`), a decision question set outside the bounds
(`400`, `invalid_decision_questions`), a body whose fields disagree with
its `kind` (`400`, `invalid_body`), an input estimate over the ceiling
(`413`), the same key with a different body (`409`), a document that never
satisfied the caller's schema (`503`, `verdict_schema_violation`), no
decision-capable route (`503`, `decision_unavailable`), an unavailable
verdict producer, catalog, database or provider (`503`), and a deadline
that passed before a route was chosen (`504`).

Returns only after the settlement transaction has committed.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Required. Replaying a key returns the stored run and never charges twice.

200.description: The verdict, validated against the caller's schema, or a stored run replayed with its verdict

202.description: The run is in flight and was observed from its durable state

400.description: Malformed body, a missing or invalid idempotency key, or a verdict schema outside the bounds

401.description: Missing, malformed, or expired bearer token

403.description: The verified identity lacks the required scope

409.description: The same idempotency key was replayed with a different body

413.description: The body exceeds the size cap, or the input exceeds the token ceiling

503.description: A required dependency is unavailable, or the verdict never satisfied the schema

504.description: The deadline passed before a route was chosen

get.summary: Reads one run from durable state, with its verdict when it has one.
get.description:
Never calls a provider, whatever the run's state: an in-flight run is
reported, not resumed by a second call.

200.description: The run as durable state has it, carrying its verdict when it reached one

400.description: The run id is not a valid identifier

401.description: Missing, malformed, or expired bearer token

403.description: The verified identity lacks the required scope

404.description: No such run for this tenant

503.description: The durable store is unavailable

get.description:
This route reads durable state and **never** performs a provider call, so
observing a run cannot charge for it. It emits one `state` event for the
run's current state and, when the run is terminal, one `terminal` event
carrying the digests and — for a completed run — the validated verdict,
then closes.

# Why this is an observation stream and not a token relay

It was already not a token relay, for a reason the pivot makes stronger
rather than weaker. **A validated verdict cannot be streamed as a verdict.**
Validation is a property of the whole document: until the last byte has
arrived there is no document to check against the caller's schema, so any
token emitted earlier is a byte this service has not proved satisfies the
contract it promised. Streaming those bytes under the same endpoint would
be a stream that lies about what it is — the client would be parsing a
candidate while the API's own guarantee is that it only ever returns
documents that passed.

The honest shapes are the two this route already has: an observation
stream over durable state, which is what this is, or a separate endpoint
for *unvalidated* candidate tokens, which would be a different product
promise and a contract change nobody has asked for. So the verdict appears
here once, whole, in the terminal frame — after settlement, which is the
same rule `create_run` obeys.

200.description: Server-sent events describing the run's durable state; a completed run's terminal frame carries the whole validated verdict, never partial tokens

400.description: The run id is not a valid identifier

401.description: Missing, malformed, or expired bearer token

403.description: The verified identity lacks the required scope

404.description: No such run for this tenant

503.description: The durable store is unavailable

get.summary: An organization's usage rollup over a window.
get.description:
Refuses a caller without the usage-read scope, a window whose bounds are not
UTC RFC 3339 second-precision timestamps, a window whose bounds are out of
order, and one bound supplied without the other. Every figure is aggregated
from durable accounting rows inside one transaction, so a dashboard refresh
during an in-flight run sees a consistent snapshot rather than a partial sum.

403.description: The identity lacks the usage read scope

503.description: Accounting storage is not configured or unreachable

get.summary: The spend and token ledger: one entry per provider call, newest first.
get.description:
Refuses the same malformed windows as the rollup, and a `limit` of zero. A
`limit` above the documented cap is clamped, not refused. Entries come from
the append-only attempt table, so an entry never changes after it is
written and a reconciled attempt appears as its own row.

never distinguishes "not yours" from "does not exist".

ApiErrorBody.description: The fixed error envelope from `docs/CONVENTIONS.md` section 2.

code.description: Stable snake_case identifier a client may branch on.

message.description: For humans. Never assembled from provider output.

request_id.description: Always present so a report can be traced.

retryable.description:
Present only on a quota refusal, where whether waiting can help is the
one thing the client needs beyond the code. Absent everywhere else, so
the envelope every other route emits is exactly the documented three
fields.

code.description: The one-time authorization code from the WorkOS redirect.

CapabilityHint.description:
The capability vocabulary a caller may hint with.

A wire mirror of `opentype_catalog::Capability` rather than a re-export:
`opentype-catalog` is a domain crate and does not derive `ToSchema`, and
`docs/CONVENTIONS.md` section 1 says a type needed by the edge does not
travel *into* a lower crate to get there. The mapping below is exhaustive,
so adding a catalog capability fails to compile here until the wire
vocabulary and the OpenAPI document are updated with it — which is what a
contract change should feel like.

CostBasis.description:
Where the `cost_micros` figure beside a verdict came from.

This field exists because the honest answer is not always the same one, and
presenting an estimate as a measurement is the defect it closes. A provider
that reports its own billable usage gives us `provider_reported`; a provider
that reports nothing leaves the catalog's price arithmetic as the only
figure there is, and that is `estimated` — named, rather than passed off as
what the call cost.

A caller reconciling an invoice needs this distinction: summing `estimated`
rows against a provider statement will not balance, and a field that did
not say so would make that look like our accounting error rather than the
absence of a provider figure.

role.description:
Must be a role this service maps, checked before WorkOS is called so an
invitation cannot be created for a role that would grant nothing.

name.description: Human label shown in the console. Not a credential and not unique.

scopes.description:
Requested scopes. Refused with `403` if the creating account does not
hold every one of them.

oneOf.description:
Which identity the key acts as. Omitted means the calling user, which is
the console's default for a personal key.

CreateRunRequest.description:
A run submission.

There is no `model` field and no `provider` field. Model ids are catalog
data and the route is the router's decision; an arbitrary client-supplied
model id has nowhere to arrive. `capability_hint` is the one thing a caller
may say about routing, and it is drawn from a closed vocabulary rather than
free text — see [`CreateRunRequest::capability_hint`].

# Why this is one flat struct and not two, or an enum

A run is a verdict or a decision, and the valid field set depends on which.
That is strictly worse to read than two structs, and it is what the
compatibility guarantee costs. Spelling it as a serde internally-tagged
enum — the obvious answer — is refused on measured evidence: `#[serde(tag =
"kind")]` makes the tag **required**, so every caller written against the
committed `openapi.json`, where `CreateRunRequest.required` is
`["messages", "schema", "max_output_tokens"]` and no `kind` exists, would
start failing at `400`. A contract that breaks every existing client to add
a variant is a versioning event, not an addition.

So: a flat struct, `deny_unknown_fields` kept, an optional defaulted
discriminant, and cross-field validation at admission. The "wrong field for
this kind" message moves from serde to us, where it is a `400` with a
stable code — which is what a client can branch on anyway.

`schema` moves from required to optional **in the struct only**. It stays
required *for a verdict*, enforced by [`admit_contract`], so no verdict
caller's observable contract changes. `openapi.json` carries that in prose,
because `required` cannot express it.

kind.description:
Which kind of answer this run produces. Absent means
[`RunKind::Verdict`], which is what every request written before
decisions existed means.

messages.description:
The prompt turns. Required for a verdict; forbidden for a decision,
whose input is `state`.

schema.description:
The JSON Schema the verdict must satisfy. Required **for a verdict**: a
verdict run with no schema has no verdict to produce, and prose is not
a product here. Forbidden for a decision.

Bounded and compiled at admission before a run row exists. A schema
outside the bounds is `400` with code `invalid_verdict_schema` and
nothing is created, nothing reserved, no provider called.

state.description:
The thing being decided about. Any JSON; an object is first-class.
Required for a decision, forbidden for a verdict.

instructions.description: Schema-level context, the decision path's analogue of `system`.

questions.description:
The questions, keyed by the caller's own ids. Required for a decision.

A `BTreeMap` on the wire, which is what JSON gives us, plus
[`CreateRunRequest::question_order`] to recover the caller's own order
— see that field for why the order matters and cannot be inferred.

draws.description:
How many independent noise draws to average, `1..=8`, default 1.

A fixed integer only. The companion server also accepts `"auto"`, which
takes one read and then decides whether to take more based on what that
read looked like — making the provider choose the spend. Every
accounting rule here points the other way (`charge_verdict_attempt`:
"never from anything a provider returned"), so `"auto"` is refused
rather than approximated.

Draws multiply cost. They are worth paying for when you threshold the
probability and the value lands near the threshold; not worth it when
you consume the argmax and never compare the number to anything.

think_tokens.description:
Thought tokens the read may generate first, `0..=4096`, default 0. A
real quality knob with a legible price: they are generated tokens.

capability_hint.description:
Optional routing hint from the closed [`CapabilityHint`] vocabulary.

**Additive only.** It can narrow the candidate set; it can never widen
a ceiling, extend a deadline, or make an ineligible candidate eligible.
A caller who needs a vision-capable or reasoning-capable model says so
here; the schema cannot tell us that.

max_output_tokens.description:
Output tokens this run may generate. Priced separately from input, so it
is part of the spend estimate rather than a hint.

deadline_ms.description:
Time budget in milliseconds. Clamped to [`MAX_DEADLINE_MS`]; absent
means [`DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS`].

question_order.description:
The caller's own question order, when it matters to them.

JSON objects have no order a `BTreeMap` preserves, and the question
order **is** the row order of the answer template the provider builds.
Absent means "the sorted order is fine"; present, it must name exactly
the keys of `questions`, and the questions are sent in that order.

A separate field rather than a silent guess, because the alternative is
worse in both directions: sorting silently reorders a template the
caller wrote, and there is no way to recover an original order a
`BTreeMap` already discarded. Forbidden for a verdict.

CurrentSessionResponse.description:
The current session as the console reads it. No token is echoed here: the
caller already holds its own bearer, and returning it would put a credential
in a `GET` response for no reason.

oneOf.description: Optional descriptions of what each side means.

allOf.description: A yes/no question. The answer is P(yes).

oneOf.description: A yes/no question. The answer is P(yes).

allOf.description:
A closed option set: option name to an optional description. The name
is what an answer and an `ask_if` compare against.

oneOf.description:
A closed option set: option name to an optional description. The name
is what an answer and an `ask_if` compare against.

allOf.description:
An ordered set of levels. The order is the level order, and the index
is the meaningful key of the answer.

oneOf.description:
An ordered set of levels. The order is the level order, and the index
is the meaningful key of the answer.

DecisionQuestionRequest.description:
One question of a decision, discriminated on `type`.

Internally tagged, unlike [`CreateRunRequest`]'s own `kind`, and the
asymmetry is deliberate: `type` has always been required on a question —
there is no legacy caller to break — and this is exactly the case an
internally-tagged enum is for, three variants whose `criteria` means three
different things. The companion server's `jev_schema` validates precisely
this, per type.

DecisionReadResponse.description:
What constrained a decision's answers.

The decision path's [`SchemaEnforcementResponse`], and it answers the same
question: was the answer provider-enforced or reconstructed? A separate
vocabulary rather than two more enforcement variants, because a caller
reading `enforced` on a decision would reasonably think a schema had been
checked, and none was.

DecisionResponse.description:
One question's answer set, as a client sees it.

A decision's answers are the response, the way a verdict's document is.
`answers` is keyed by the caller's own question ids and each value is
discriminated on `type`, so a caller reads the shape that matches the
question they asked.

The per-answer shapes are documented on the wire rather than here, because
they come from the provider's own vocabulary; the ones worth knowing before
reading a number:

- a `noul` answer's `probability` is **P(yes)**, not "the probability of
  the answer", and carries no confidence — with two labels confidence
  would be `max(p, 1 - p)`, a field a caller can compute and that could
  therefore disagree with itself;
- a `score` is **0-indexed** with a `legend`, and its `probabilities` are
  keyed by legend index while a `choice`'s are keyed by option name. That
  asymmetry is inherited from the surface whose vocabulary this adopted,
  and it is kept and documented rather than smoothed over: a score's
  levels are ordered, so the index *is* the meaningful key;
- `label_mass` and `answered_within_labels`, where present, are the
  honesty rule applied to a probability. When `answered_within_labels` is
  false the reported probabilities are a renormalisation over labels the
  model did not favour at all, and a confident-looking `0.71` with no way
  to see that is exactly the defect this product exists not to commit;
- a skipped question is `{"type": "skipped", "because": {...}}` rather than
  a null, because here the null *is* meaningful and the meaning belongs in
  the value rather than in a side-channel to join against.

**No `stderr` or `agreement` field exists, at any draw count.** The
upstream surface computes both and then drops them before they reach the
wire, so this service has nothing to report — and reporting a zero, or
reconstructing a standard error from a single reported mean, would be a
claim of precision from data that never arrived. See
`opentype_provider::decision_read::DecisionOutcome::draw_statistics_are_available`.

answers.description:
One answer per question, keyed by the caller's own question ids.

Typed as raw JSON because the per-answer shape is discriminated on
`type` and differs per question type; the values are not provider text
but numbers this service decoded field by field through
`opentype_provider::decision_read::DecisionAnswer`, with every
probability range-checked.

draws.description: How many independent noise draws were averaged.

model.description:
The catalog model id that served the read.

Returned, unlike on a verdict, because a probability without the model
that produced it is not reproducible and not comparable across runs.

stages.description:
The stage schedule the read actually ran in: question ids per stage,
each stage after the stages of everything its questions depend on.

thought_tokens.description:
Thought tokens generated before the read, when the caller funded any.

The thought **text** is never returned. It is raw provider prose, and
`docs/CONVENTIONS.md` section 7 forbids populating a response field
from a raw provider payload. The count and the closed flag are facts
about the read; the prose is a payload nobody validated or promised.

ErrorBody.description: The fixed error envelope from `docs/CONVENTIONS.md` section 2.

code.description: Stable snake_case identifier a client may branch on.

message.description: For humans. Never assembled from provider output.

request_id.description: Always present so a report can be traced.

oneOf.description: A human member. The value is the WorkOS user identifier.

id.description: A human member. The value is the WorkOS user identifier.

oneOf.description: A machine identity owned by the organization.

id.description: A machine identity owned by the organization.

KeyPrincipal.description:
Who a key acts as.

The service-account model in one type. A key issued to a `User` dies with
that user's membership: remove the member and their keys are revoked in the
same transaction, because a credential that outlives the human who owns it
is how an offboarded contractor keeps production access. A key issued to a
`ServiceAccount` is owned by the organization, survives the person who
created it, and is what a deployment should actually use — which is why
creation records `created_by` separately from the principal.

KeyResponse.description: A key without its secret. Every read path returns this shape.

secret_prefix.description: The visible fragment, e.g. `otsk_a1b2c3d4`. Never the whole secret.

KeyState.description:
Lifecycle of a key. A revoked key is never deleted: the row is the audit
trail for everything the key did, and deleting it would orphan those
records.

secret.description:
The plaintext secret. Shown once. The service stores only its SHA-256
and cannot return this value again; a lost secret is rotated, not
recovered.

KeyWithSecretResponse.description:
The only response in the API that carries a secret, and the only one that
ever will. Returned by create and rotate; a second `GET` on the same key
returns [`KeyResponse`], with no secret, forever.

LedgerEntryBody.description: One ledger row on the wire.

LedgerParams.description: `GET /v1/usage/ledger` parameters: a window plus a row cap.

MemberRemovedResponse.description:
What removing a member actually did. The key count is here because the
destructive part of removal is invisible otherwise.

permissions.description:
The permissions this membership's role grants in this service. Reported
so the console can hide actions it would be refused, without hardcoding
the mapping in TypeScript.

NoulCriteria.description: What a `noul` question's two sides mean.

OrganizationRole.description:
Organization roles, ordered: every role is at least as privileged as the one
below it. The ordering is the whole point — [`Role::outranks_or_equals`] is
what stops a member from promoting themselves.

`ServiceAccount` is deliberately *not* a role. A service account is a
principal that holds keys; its permissions are the scopes on those keys, and
those scopes were bounded by a human's role at creation time. Giving a
service account a role of its own would create a second ladder to climb.

Named `OrganizationRole` in the OpenAPI document. `api/auth.rs` also has a
`Role`, and that one is an open WorkOS slug string rather than this closed
ladder; `components(schemas(...))` keys on the type name, so without this
the two would share one schema and a client would be handed whichever
definition was registered last.

Permission.description:
An application permission. This is the vocabulary a route demands; a WorkOS
role is only ever an input to [`Role::permissions`].

Adding a variant is a contract change: it is a lowercase snake_case string on
the wire and needs a re-emitted `openapi.json`.

QuotaLimitsBody.description:
The limits half of `GET /v1/quota`. A null limit is "no organization-level
limit is configured"; `request_spend_ceiling_micros` is never null.

request_spend_ceiling_micros.description:
The effective per-request provider spend ceiling after the
architecture's ceiling, configuration, and the organization's own row
have all been applied. An over-estimate request is refused with `429`.

remaining_spend_micros.description: Null when the matching limit is not configured.

organization_id.description:
Switch the active organization while refreshing. This is how an
organization switch is performed: a new access token is minted with the
new `org_id`, so permissions are re-derived from the new membership
rather than carried over.

Role.description:
A WorkOS role slug as it appears on an organization membership.

Roles are configured in WorkOS, so this is an opaque string rather than an
enum: a role the deployment has not mapped must not become a compile error
in a running service, it must become *no permissions*.

RoleListResponse.description:
The role catalog, so a client can populate an invitation form without
guessing which slugs this service maps.

RunCounts.description: Run counts by terminal state, for the dashboard header.

in_flight.description: Admitted and not yet terminal. Their reservations are held, not settled.

RunKind.description:
Which kind of answer a run produces.

`docs/DECISIONS-decision-runs.md` section 4, in one sentence: a verdict
asks the model to write a document and then checks the document; a decision
asks the model for its distribution over a closed answer set it was never
able to leave.

The corollary, which is why both exist: a verdict can express anything a
JSON Schema can and gives you no calibration; a decision can express only
yes/no, a closed option set, or an ordered level, and gives you a number
you can threshold.

RunListResponse.description:
A page of runs. `Eq` is absent because a [`RunResponse`] may carry a
verdict, and `serde_json::Value` holds floats, for which equality is
partial. `PartialEq` is what a test needs and it is what the data supports.

limit.description:
What was asked for after clamping, so a client can tell that its
oversized `limit` was tightened rather than honoured.

RunMessage.description:
One turn of the prompt. Deliberately minimal: a client cannot express a
provider-specific parameter here, so nothing can be smuggled through to an
adapter.

RunResponse.description:
A run as a client sees it.

`verdict` is the point of the response: the document the model produced and
this service validated against the caller's own schema. It is absent, never
null-and-meaningless, on a run that has not produced one — an in-flight run,
a failed run, or a listing row read without its verdict. A caller that sees
`state: "completed"` and no `verdict` is looking at a listing, not at a
finished submission.

`usage` and `cost_micros` are optional for the same reason: they are only
knowable from durable state, and a zero would be a false statement about
what the run cost rather than an admission that this response does not know.

kind.description:
Which kind of answer this run produces, so a reader knows whether to
look at `verdict` or at `decision`.

input_digest.description:
Hex SHA-256 of the normalized input, which covers the caller's schema.
The input itself is not stored.

verdict.description:
The validated verdict. Returned only after it satisfied the caller's
schema and only after settlement is durable.

A completed run carries this **or** [`Self::decision`], never both and
never neither. The invariant is not expressible in this flat struct and
is held by the handler and by the two tables' own constraints; `kind`
says which to expect.

oneOf.description:
The decision's answer set. Returned only after settlement is durable,
on the same terms as [`Self::verdict`].

Whether `cost_micros` is a provider-reported figure or this service's
own estimate. Present exactly when `cost_micros` is, because a cost with
no stated basis is the defect this field closes.

What constrained the verdict: the provider's own schema enforcement, or
nothing but this service's validation. Present on a response that
carries a verdict produced by a call made for this request.

Absent on a replay and on a listing row. That is not an oversight: the
value is a property of the wire exchange, and `run_verdicts` stores the
document and its cost, not the enforcement the adapter observed. An
invented value here would be worse than its absence — see
[`replayed_with_verdict`].

replayed.description:
True when this response came from storage rather than from a provider
call made for this request. A replayed idempotency key is never a second
charge.

RunsErrorBody.description:
The error body shape from `docs/CONVENTIONS.md` section 2. `message` is for
humans and is never assembled from provider output.

Named `RunsErrorBody` in the OpenAPI document: `api/auth.rs` declares its
own `ErrorBody` of the same shape, and `components(schemas(...))` keys on
the type name, so one of the two would otherwise silently stand for both.

code.description: Stable snake_case identifier clients may branch on.

violations.description:
JSON Pointer paths naming where the model's document failed the
caller's schema, at most [`opentype_neo::MAX_REPORTED_POINTERS`] of
them. Present only on `verdict_schema_violation`.

These are derived from the caller's own schema and the caller's own
document, never from provider text, so this does not breach the rule
that an error body is never assembled from provider output. It is the
difference between "it failed" and "your `/risk/score` came back as a
string".

SchemaEnforcementResponse.description:
What actually constrained the answer this run returned.

A wire mirror of [`opentype_provider::SchemaEnforcement`] rather than a
re-export, for the same reason [`CapabilityHint`] mirrors
`opentype_catalog::Capability`: `opentype-provider` is a domain crate and
does not derive `ToSchema`, and `docs/CONVENTIONS.md` section 1 says a type
the edge needs does not travel *into* a lower crate to get there. The
mapping below is exhaustive, so a new provider-side variant fails to
compile here until the wire vocabulary and the OpenAPI document carry it.

This is the visible half of the fact that the provider families are **not**
uniform, and it is why the value reaches a client at all. Without it an
answer a provider guaranteed and an answer we merely asked for and then
validated ourselves are indistinguishable. What each value means to a
caller, and specifically what a *future* validation failure against the
same model would mean:

| Value | What bound the answer | A validation failure would be |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unconstrained` | Nothing: no schema travelled, or the family could only ask and the model answered outside the schema slot anyway. | Expected. This service's own validation was the only check. |
| `requested` | The schema went in the family's slot and the model was invited to use it; the family cannot compel it. | Expected. The model was free to ignore the schema. |
| `forced` | The model was compelled into the schema slot, but the provider did not itself check the arguments against the schema. | Possible. The shape was asked for, not verified upstream. |
| `enforced` | The provider constrained decoding to the schema. | A provider defect worth reporting upstream, not an expected outcome. |

Every verdict this service returns has passed validation regardless of the
value here — the guarantee is unconditional. What the value adds is whether
that guarantee rested on the provider or on us.

Scope.description:
One capability a token may authorize.

This is the vocabulary every route demands, and it is disjoint from
`api::admin`'s operator permission namespace on purpose: no tenant scope can
name an operator capability, so no tenant token can reach the operator
surface.

Adding a variant is a contract change: it is a lowercase snake_case string
on the wire and needs a re-emitted `openapi.json`.

SessionToken.description:
A session token in transit — an authorization code, a refresh token, or an
access token being handed to the caller that owns the session.

It exists so that a token can cross this boundary without ever becoming
loggable: `Debug` is redacted, and the value is reachable only through
[`SessionToken::expose`] at the moment an outbound WorkOS request is built.
Unlike the configuration `Secret`, this one is `Deserialize`/`Serialize`,
because the sign-in exchange is exactly the place where a token is a
request field and a response field. It is never written to a database, never
placed in an error variant, and never put in a tracing field.

SharedQuestionFields.description:
The fields every question type shares.

Flattened into each variant rather than repeated, so a field added here
cannot reach two of the three types and miss the third.

depends_on.description:
Other questions in this set whose answers this question's stage must
come after. Stages are the caller's own logic and cannot be emulated
client-side without paying for two runs.

ask_if.description:
Question id to the answer names that make this question worth asking.
A question whose condition fails is `skipped` rather than answered.

alone.description:
Whether this question must be read on its own rather than jointly with
its stage. A one-bit escape hatch that is impossible to reconstruct
client-side.

redirect_uri.description: Where WorkOS returns the browser after sign-in.

state.description: Opaque CSRF state the client will compare on return.

organization_id.description: Sign straight into one organization instead of letting the user pick.

authorization_url.description: The WorkOS-hosted URL to redirect the browser to.

SpendTotals.description:
Spend totals in micro-USD, from `budget_reservations` and
`provider_attempts`.

reserved_micros.description: Held against a ceiling, whether or not it has settled yet.

unsettled_micros.description:
Reserved and not yet settled: in-flight runs and attempts awaiting
reconciliation.

refresh_token.description:
Required: switching mints a new access token, which needs the refresh
token. Re-signing the current token would let a revoked membership keep
its permissions until expiry.

TokenTotals.description: Token totals, summed over settled attempts.

UsageResponse.description:
Token usage as it was settled. Never estimated when the provider reported
it.

UsageWindowParams.description:
The window every read accepts. Both bounds are optional and must be given
together; omitting them reads the organization's current quota period.
